title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-RAM algorithm that, for every finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arbitrary real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(n+m)\) worst-case total time, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\)? The graph is explicitly listed, and weights are opaque keys that may only be copied and compared. The machine, output and quantifier conventions are fixed below; the bound counts all computation, not only weight comparisons.
definitions:
Instance and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with \(G=(V,E)\) connected. Write \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). Each \(e\in E\) has a weight \(w(e)\in\mathbb R\), with no integrality, magnitude, distinctness or sign promise. A spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \((V,T)\) is connected and has no cycle; necessarily \(|T|=n-1\). Its weight is the finite real sum \(W(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A minimum spanning tree satisfies
\[\forall T'\subseteq E\text{ that is a spanning tree}:\quad W(T)\le W(T').\]
Connectedness ensures a spanning tree exists, and the finite collection of trees has a minimum. For \(n=1\), the graph has no edges and the required output is the empty tree. Equal or negative edge weights are allowed, and any minimizing tree is accepted. The algorithm need not output the numerical sum.

Explicit input and output. Input records give \(n,m\), the list of vertex labels, and an ordered list of \(m\) edge records. Edge \(j\), for \(1\le j\le m\), has endpoints \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and a handle for its opaque weight key. Pairs are not repeated, but their list order is arbitrary. The index \(j\) is the edge's distinct identifier. The input occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) constant-size records. It is a full graph description rather than a circuit or oracle generating a larger graph. A weight key is supplied as an abstract atom, not a finite precision approximation or a binary expansion of its real value. The output lists exactly \(n-1\) distinct valid edge identifiers forming a minimum tree, in any order. No behavior is required on malformed or disconnected inputs.

Weight access. A weight handle can be stored, copied or retrieved in constant time. An instruction given two such handles returns their exact three-way real comparison: less, equal or greater. That instruction costs one operation independently of the real numbers. These are the only observations of weight values available to the algorithm. Weight handles identify their edge records; their numerical identifiers encode no information about the values. The program cannot inspect a weight's bits, add or subtract weights, multiply them, convert them to integers, hash their numerical representations, or compare arithmetic expressions involving weights. Copying a handle does not manufacture a new numerical key. The sum \(W(T)\) defines mathematical correctness, not an allowed machine instruction.

Nonweight machine operations. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\), and for input parameter \(N\) uses unsigned words of
\[\ell=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits for vertex labels, edge identifiers, counters and memory addresses. A word represents an integer from zero to \(2^\ell-1\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially zero; weight-key storage can equivalently keep the corresponding input handles. The input is read-only, and output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction touches a constant number of words or handles. Reading, writing, copying, comparing nonweight words and conditional branching cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^\ell\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT are also unit-cost. Logical shifts by fewer than \(\ell\) positions discard bits outside the word and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(\ell\) returns zero. Larger integer calculations require multiple words and their operations are charged. The program may use \(\ell\) as the machine word length. Word arithmetic is not arithmetic on the represented real weights.

Uniformity and time. There is no random input, random instruction, input-size advice, free preprocessing table or external computational oracle. The same finite program and word constant are used on every instance and edge-list order. All initialization it performs, comparisons, ordinary computation, generated tables and writing every output identifier count. Let \(T_A(G,w)\) be the number of these operations, with the edge-list representation understood as part of the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct tree on every valid instance. The time requirement is
\[\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall(G,w)\text{ with }n+m\ge N_0:\quad T_A(G,w)\le C(n+m).\]
The constants are independent of the graph, weights, density and representation order. This is deterministic worst-case sequential time. It is not an expectation over random graphs or over random choices, and an unbounded slowly growing extra factor does not count as linear.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic program and fixed word constant and prove termination, spanning-tree feasibility, exact minimum total weight and the displayed total-time bound for every connected simple graph and all real weight assignments. The proof must cover repeated and negative weights and the single-vertex case. If it uses decision trees or lookup tables, all work needed to produce and use them must be included.

A negative answer must rule out every correct deterministic program in the specified comparison-RAM model. Equivalently, for every word constant and every program that halts with a minimum tree on every valid input, prove that for each \(C>0\) and each \(N_0\) there is a valid instance and edge-list order with \(n+m\ge N_0\) on which the time exceeds \(C(n+m)\). A lower bound for one particular algorithm, one data structure, or a stricter pointer-only model does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound must identify its unproved assumption and is not an unconditional resolution.

Expected-linear randomized algorithms, deterministic integer-weight algorithms that inspect weight bits, restricted graph classes and a linear number of comparisons with superlinear control overhead do not alone meet the target. Optimality relative to an unknown decision-tree complexity must include a linear bound on that complexity and the necessary implementation overhead to establish an affirmative answer. This card requires an exact minimum tree and an actual linear bound, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

importance.reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.

progress.text: Fredman–Willard obtain deterministic linear time in a stronger integer-word model.
Karger–Klein–Tarjan obtain randomized linear time for arbitrary comparison weights.
Pettie–Ramachandran match the optimal decision-tree complexity with a uniform deterministic algorithm, without determining that complexity.
Pettie–Ramachandran develop alternative randomized MST algorithms using far fewer random bits; complete deterministic linear time remains unresolved.
Doron and coauthors discuss MST in a pseudorandomness framework, explicitly distinguishing this illustration from an improved deterministic MST running-time bound.

The May 2026 pseudorandomness manuscript explicitly treats MST as motivation and does not improve the known deterministic frontier. Integer-weight access, randomized expectation, high-girth restrictions, unknown optimal decision-tree complexity and distributed message bounds do not settle this card. Source limitations and inspected locators are recorded; external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is a basic optimization problem used in network design and clustering. The optimum can already be found in polynomial time; the unsettled issue is whether its exact deterministic computational cost can be only a constant multiple of the \(n\) vertex records and \(m\) edge records in the input.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for classical algorithms, but produces more information than the requested output. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The comparison lower bound for sorting all keys therefore does not automatically give a superlinear lower bound for this graph problem.

The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle's deterministic comparison algorithm runs in \(O(m\alpha(m,n))\) time, apart from the trivial one-vertex case, where \(\alpha\) is an inverse-Ackermann function. It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. The question asks for a constant overhead over input size, rather than a bound that is effectively small on practical instances.

Pettie and Ramachandran relate total deterministic computational cost to the optimal worst-case edge-comparison decision-tree complexity of the minimum spanning forest problem. Their construction is uniform: the cost of building and using small optimal decision trees is part of the analysis. For the present connected-graph problem, input reading and explicit output also remain charged. The resulting optimality theorem does not determine whether the worst-case bound is linear or slightly superlinear.

Eisenstat and coauthors distinguish two different girth restrictions. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with acyclic graphs assigned infinite girth. Their conditional reductions show equivalence of the unrestricted linear-time question with its restriction to any fixed lower bound on girth, and also with a suitably sparse family having at most \(3n/2\) edges. Their actual linear-time theorem assumes a girth threshold that grows with \(n\), according to an inverse-Ackermann variant. That size-dependent restriction leaves the general question unresolved.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

Pettie and Ramachandran also give randomized linear-time algorithms consuming far fewer random bits than the original sampling method. Reducing the number of random choices while preserving an expected time bound does not provide one deterministic program with a linear worst-case guarantee.

Doron and coauthors use minimum spanning tree as a motivating example in their May 2026 work on pseudorandomness for insensitive algorithms. Section 10.1 explicitly says that the existing deterministic near-linear MST algorithms are more efficient than the derandomizations expected from their results. The paper therefore supplies recent context on randomness reduction, not a new deterministic linear-time MST theorem.

category_assignment.reason: The target is deterministic linear-time construction of a minimum spanning tree on a static weighted graph.

sentences: The problem asks for an exact minimum spanning tree of every connected simple undirected graph with arbitrary real edge weights.
The target is one uniform deterministic sequential algorithm whose worst-case total running time is linear in the explicitly listed vertices and edges.
Weights are opaque comparison keys, while ordinary logarithmic-word computation, preprocessing and writing the output are all charged.
A complete Lean proof must establish every correctness and running-time guarantee or rule out all correct algorithms in this model.

Randomized linear time, integer-weight algorithms and uniform decision-tree optimality are known, but the checked 2026 literature does not settle deterministic linear time for arbitrary comparison weights.

source_formulation.text: The inherited card selects the classical uniform sequential comparison question: all connected simple graphs, arbitrary opaque real weights and deterministic worst-case O(n+m) total time. Karger–Klein–Tarjan explicitly distinguish this weight-access model from the integer representation model, and Pettie–Ramachandran distinguish optimal comparison complexity from a known linear time bound. The review specifies the exact machine instructions, output, constants and complete Lean criterion while preserving the target, category and importance.

checked_sources: Read Karger–Klein–Tarjan author manuscript full abstract, introduction and §1.1. The model is a sequential unit-cost RAM whose only operations on edge weights are comparisons. The algorithm is randomized with linear bounds; the manuscript date is 7 July 1994 and JACM publication is 1995. Its tie handling and no-isolated-vertices forest convention were distinguished from this connected graph card.

The Chazelle source PDF text extraction is unreadable because of font encoding. Rendered and visually inspected its first page: JACM 47(6),2000,1028–1047; deterministic O(m alpha(m,n)); comparison pointer machine; no numerical assumptions on edge costs. The introduction explicitly distinguishes randomized linear time and integer-bit linear time from the remaining comparison target. Did not claim to read or certify the entire proof.

Read Pettie–Ramachandran JACM 2002 full abstract and introduction, §4 decision-tree construction, §5 definition of T*(m,n) as worst-case MSF comparison complexity and Theorem 5.8, and §6 implementation discussion. Uniform generation of small trees is charged. Their optimality theorem does not determine the asymptotic decision-tree function; input-reading and output costs remain explicit in the card.

Read Fredman–Willard publisher abstract and 1994 JCSS metadata through the primary indexed page; direct open returned 403 and the original full proof was not inspected. Corroborated the integer-word/weight-bit model distinction in the full primary Karger–Klein–Tarjan and Pettie–Ramachandran introductions. No real-key comparison consequence was inferred.

Read the undated Eisenstat–Moshkovitz–Tarjan–Xu author manuscript full introduction, Corollary 1, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1. The sparse threshold is 3n/2; each fixed girth restriction is conditionally sufficient for the general question, whereas the proved algorithm requires girth b(t,log n) for fixed t>1. The paper explicitly notes the remaining gap. A recent web crawl timestamp was not used as a publication date.

Read Pettie–Ramachandran published 2008 coauthor-hosted PDF full abstract and introduction after the inherited Michigan URL failed certificate/timeout access. Official ACM metadata confirms TALG 4(1),Article 5,27 pages. The result reduces randomness while preserving expected efficiency; it does not remove all randomness with a worst-case linear guarantee.

Read Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman ECCC TR26-082 revision 1 abstract and full §10.1 pp.47–48. Official revision 17May 2026 fixes a typesetting error. The MST discussion explicitly says existing deterministic near-linear methods outperform the derandomization bounds expected from their work; no unconditional linear algorithm is asserted.

Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching deterministic linear comparison algorithm or lower bound. July arXiv:2607.13284 concerns approximate MST in doubling metrics; March arXiv:2603.12156 concerns distributed resources. The September 8 Algorithms 19(9)770 source was screened through its abstract and model description: its claimed linear bound counts distributed messages, not sequential local computation. These different targets were not promoted as solutions. No archive bodies were opened and external proofs were not independently certified.

Checked exact optimum versus numerical weight sum, opaque-key access versus integer operations, uniform tables, fixed machine word constant, all input orders, repeated/negative weights, singleton output and the complete all-algorithm lower-bound quantifiers. Category and selected binary target were preserved.
